title_en: Nikola Tesla: Brilliance Without a Business Plan
description_ru: История изобретателя, подарившего миру переменный ток, и его трагического неумения превращать великие идеи в деньги.
text:
When Nikola Tesla stepped off a ship in New York in 1884, he reportedly had four cents in his pocket, a book of poems and a letter of introduction to Thomas Edison. The letter contained one sentence of lasting fame: "I know two great men and you are one of them. The other is this young man." Whether Edison truly deserved the compliment is a matter for debate. What is beyond dispute is that the young man would go on to reshape how the modern world is powered, and that he would die almost penniless.

He was born in 1856 in the village of Smiljan, then part of the Austrian Empire and now in Croatia, into a Serbian Orthodox family. His father was a priest who hoped that his son would follow him into the Church. Nikola had other ideas. As a child he was haunted by vivid flashes of light and images that appeared before his eyes, and he later claimed that he could see an entire machine in his mind, test it, and detect flaws in its design before he built anything. Many people took the claim as an exaggeration, but his later work suggests that he had a remarkable gift for visualisation.

After studying engineering in Graz, Tesla worked in Budapest on a new telephone exchange, and it was in a Budapest park in 1882, while reciting Goethe, that the solution to a problem that had been haunting him suddenly arrived. He picked up a stick and sketched in the dirt the design of a motor driven by a rotating magnetic field, powered by alternating current. Such a motor needed no fragile brushes and could run smoothly for years. The idea would eventually prove worth many millions of dollars.

In New York he worked briefly for Edison, who was then the best-known inventor in America and a passionate advocate of direct current. The partnership was doomed. Tesla was a polished, fastidious European who read in several languages and dressed immaculately; Edison was a pragmatic tinkerer who trusted experiment over theory. A famous story, whose details are disputed, holds that Edison promised a fifty-thousand-dollar bonus for improving his generators, then dismissed the offer as an American joke. Tesla resigned in disgust.

His luck changed when he met investors who set up the Tesla Electric Light Company, and later the industrialist George Westinghouse, who bought the rights to his alternating-current patents in 1888 for cash and a royalty on every unit of horsepower. Thus began the so-called War of the Currents. Edison, whose business depended on direct current, ran a campaign of public demonstrations that were designed to frighten the public by showing how deadly alternating current could be. Yet alternating current had a decisive economic advantage: it could be sent over long distances at high voltage and then reduced for safe use at home.

Westinghouse won the argument in 1893, when his company illuminated the World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago with a quarter of a million lamps, and in 1895 the first major hydroelectric power plant at Niagara Falls began transmitting alternating current to Buffalo. Tesla, who had helped to design the system, was in his late thirties and famous. He lived in a suite in a Manhattan hotel, dined with celebrities and gave lectures in which he passed hundreds of thousands of volts through his body without harm, delighting audiences who could not tell that the current was of a frequency too high to injure him.

Ironically, Tesla's greatest financial decision was an act of generosity. When Westinghouse's company teetered on the edge of bankruptcy in the early 1890s, he tore up the royalty agreement that would have made Tesla a multimillionaire. Tesla felt grateful to the man who had believed in him, and had no head for money anyway. He never again managed to secure such favourable terms.

His ambitions only grew larger. He demonstrated wireless-controlled boats, designed neon-like lighting and invented the Tesla coil, a resonant transformer still used in radio equipment and, more theatrically, in science museums. Then he conceived the project that would break him: a tall tower at Wardenclyffe on Long Island that would transmit information, and even power, across the globe without wires. The banker J. P. Morgan put up one hundred and fifty thousand dollars, but when Guglielmo Marconi sent a transatlantic radio signal in 1901 using cheaper methods, Morgan refused to supply more. The tower was never finished and, in 1917, it was demolished to pay debts.

The final decades were lonely. Tesla made grand announcements, including a so-called death ray, that were never backed by working prototypes, and newspapers began to treat him as an eccentric. He developed rituals bordering on obsession, such as insisting on napkins in multiples of three, and he formed an intense bond with the pigeons that he fed in city parks. He died alone in a New York hotel room in January 1943, aged eighty-six, with more than a few debts to his name.

Yet reputation tends to be generous to the neglected. In 1960 the international scientific community named the unit of magnetic flux density the tesla in his honour, and the world has since discovered that his name, like his best ideas, has a tendency to return. His story is a reminder that invention and success are not the same thing, and that a brilliant mind without a business plan may illuminate everyone but its owner.

questions.question: What did Tesla sketch in the dirt in Budapest?
questions.answer: A motor driven by a rotating magnetic field using alternating current.

questions.question: Why did Tesla leave Edison?
questions.answer: They clashed; Edison would not pay a promised bonus.

questions.question: What generous thing did Tesla do for Westinghouse?
questions.answer: He tore up the royalty agreement.

questions.question: What happened to the Wardenclyffe tower?
questions.answer: It was never finished and was demolished to pay debts.
